result:
The Weight of Small Things

I keep thinking about the way my grandmother peeled an apple. One continuous spiral, the knife never leaving the fruit, the peel falling in a single curl onto the newspaper she'd spread across the kitchen table. She did this every morning for forty years, she told me, though I only saw her do it for the three years I lived with her after my mother's surgery. The newspaper was always the *Telegram & Gazette*, always the local paper, always spread with the same careful corners tucked under the table's edge so it wouldn't slide. She read it cover to cover, every day, even the advertisements, even the sports scores for teams she didn't follow. "You never know what you'll need," she said. "Information is a kind of insurance."

I was twelve. I thought she was strange. Now I am forty-three and I find myself spreading newspaper on my kitchen table when I peel an apple, though I have never once read the paper I spread. I use it for the peel. The peel falls in a curl, though not as perfect as hers. Mine breaks. I don't mind the breaking. I have learned to mind less and less as I get older, which I think might be the same as learning to mind more, properly, the things that actually matter.

---

My father kept a jar of screws on his workbench. Not organized by size or type, just a jar, glass, with a metal lid that had rusted in a perfect circle around the rim. When he needed a screw, he would dump the jar onto the bench, find what he needed, and pour the rest back. The sound was particular. Glass on wood, then the settling, the small clinks as each screw found its place among the others. I can still hear it. I can still hear him humming, though I cannot remember what he hummed. Some country song, probably. He liked country before it was cool, before it was anything, when it was just what played on the radio in his truck.

He died in March, which is cruel, because March is the month everything comes back to life and he did not. I went to his house to help my mother sort through things. The jar was on the workbench, exactly where he'd left it. I opened it. The smell hit me first—oil and metal and something else, something organic, like the jar had been breathing. I put my hand in. The screws were warm. I know they weren't. I know this was grief, or memory, or the simple fact of a room that had been heated all winter. But they were warm. I held them for a long time. Then I put them back.

---

There is a photograph of me at seven, standing in front of a birthday cake, my face caught mid-expression, mouth open, eyes wide with the particular terror and joy of being the center of attention. I am wearing a shirt with a dinosaur on it. The dinosaur is green. I have no memory of this party. I have no memory of the shirt. But I look at the photograph and I recognize myself. Not the face, exactly, but the posture. The way I hold my shoulders, slightly forward, as if bracing for something. I still do this. I catch myself in windows, in mirrors, in the reflection of my phone screen when it goes dark. Shoulders forward. Waiting.

My mother gave me this photograph last year, along with a box of others I had never seen. Most of them are of other people. Cousins I don't know. Aunts I've forgotten. A woman in a yellow dress standing in front of a car I don't recognize, smiling at someone who is not the camera. On the back, in my mother's handwriting: *Aunt Ruth, 1962, before.* Before what, I wanted to ask. Before the divorce? Before the move? Before the thing that made her stop smiling in photographs? I didn't ask. I put the photograph in the box and closed the lid.

---

I have started keeping a list of things I don't understand. Not questions, exactly. Things. Phenomena. The way a cat will stare at a wall for twenty minutes, then suddenly bolt across the room as if pursued by something invisible. The particular silence of snow, how it changes the quality of sound in a room, makes everything feel further away. The fact that I can remember the taste of a specific cereal I ate once, at a friend's house, in 1989, but cannot remember what I had for breakfast this morning. The way my body knows things before my mind does—the way my shoulders tighten when I walk past a certain street, though I cannot say why. The way grief arrives in waves that have nothing to do with the calendar, the way it can be absent for months and then return, full force, because someone mentions a song, or a smell, or the particular angle of light in late afternoon.

I used to think understanding was the goal. Now I think it might be the obstacle. The things we understand, we file away. The things we don't understand, we carry.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 3 AM. Every night. Not a continuous bark, but a single, sharp *woof*, then silence, then another, then silence. I have come to wait for it. I lie in bed, listening for the space between the barks, and I find myself breathing in that space, holding my breath, waiting for the next one. It is a strange thing to be grateful for. But I am. The dog's bark is proof that something is awake, that the night is not empty, that there is a rhythm to the darkness that I can follow, like a rope in a black room.

I have never met the dog. I have never seen my neighbor. We share a wall, and that is all. But I know the dog's schedule better than I know my own. I know that it does not bark on rainy nights. I know that it barks more in winter, when the cold makes the sound carry differently. I know that last Tuesday, it did not bark at all, and I lay awake until 4 AM, worried, until I heard the neighbor's car start and knew that the dog was safe, was somewhere, was not lost in the dark.

---

I am learning to cook. This is not a metaphor. I mean that I am standing in my kitchen, following recipes, burning things, salting things too much, discovering that I have been pronouncing *quinoa* wrong for fifteen years. My mother cooked without recipes. She moved through the kitchen like a dancer, like someone who had internalized the music and no longer needed to hear it. I asked her once how she knew when the onions were done. "You just know," she said. "You pay attention." I am trying to pay attention. I am trying to learn the language of heat and time and transformation, the way raw things become something else, something nourishing, something that can be shared.

Last week I made soup. It was bad. Too thin, too salty, the vegetables overcooked to the point of surrender. But I ate it. I ate all of it. And as I ate, I thought about my grandmother, and her newspaper, and the way she read every word, every advertisement, every score. "You never know what you'll need," she said. I am beginning to understand. The soup was bad, but it was mine. I made it. I ate it. I will make it again, and it will be better, or it won't, but I will have made it, and that is the point, I think. That is always the point.

---

There is a tree outside my window. I don't know what kind. It has small leaves, serrated edges, and in the fall they turn a color that has no name, something between gold and rust and the particular brown of old photographs. I have watched this tree for three years. I know when it buds, when it flowers, when the leaves are full and green and the tree is heavy with its own abundance. I know when the first leaf falls, and I know that the last leaf will cling until November, until the wind finally takes it, and the branches are bare against the sky.

I used to think trees were simple. Now I think they are the most complex things I know. They grow without moving. They survive without complaining. They give shade, and fruit, and oxygen, and beauty, and they ask for nothing but time and water and the occasional attention of someone who notices them. I want to be more like this tree. I want to grow slowly, to put down roots, to offer what I can without demanding anything in return. I want to be the kind of thing that someone looks at and feels, for a moment, less alone.

---

I am running out of words. This is not a complaint. I have said what I needed to say, or what I could say, in the time I had. There are things I have not said. There are things I will not say. There is the particular weight of a life, the accumulated mass of small moments, and I have tried to give it some shape, some form, some meaning. I don't know if I have succeeded. I don't know if anyone ever does.

But I am here. I am still here. And that, I think, is enough. That is more than enough. That is everything.

The jar of screws is still on the workbench. The dog still barks at 3 AM. The tree still stands outside my window, patient, rooted, growing toward a light I cannot see. And I am here, writing, breathing, paying attention to the small things that make up a life. The peel of an apple. The warmth of metal. The particular silence of snow.

You never know what you'll need.

I am learning this. I am learning it every day.
